name: Sensing cane
tag: A telescoping cane that senses obstacles ahead and potholes below.
problem: A plain cane only reports what it touches. Drop-offs, potholes and anything above ground level go unnoticed until it is too late to react.
how: A solid-state lidar near the handle measures the distance to whatever is ahead.
An 8×8 time-of-flight imager at the tip looks down at the ground and picks out potholes and steps.
An IMU tracks how the cane is being swung, and two force sensors in the handle read the grip.
An ESP32 combines the readings and warns the user through vibration motors.
The sensor bus crosses the telescoping joint on a four-pin magnetic pogo connector, so the cane still collapses.
notes: The lidar stays on the fixed handle section, so only the I2C bus has to cross the moving joint.
Each sensor was brought up alone on the bench first; the ToF imager ran as a live heatmap before anything was integrated.
An MPU-6050 board is kept as a fallback for the IMU.

name: CNC Writer Studio
tag: A pen plotter you drive from a phone: type, draw, or teach it your handwriting.
problem: Hobby pen plotters normally need a PC running sender software and G-code prepared in advance. This one only needs a phone on its Wi-Fi.
how: An Arduino Uno with a CNC shield runs GRBL and owns every step pulse.
An ESP32-S3 hosts the Wi-Fi dashboard and streams G-code to the Uno through a ring-buffered queue.
The dashboard captures a person's handwriting and stores it as a profile in flash, so the plotter can write in that hand.
Fourteen built-in image patterns can be drawn without any external software.
A servo lifts and lowers the pen.
notes: Motion stays on GRBL on purpose. The ESP32 never generates step pulses.
A single JavaScript syntax error leaves every dashboard button dead while the wiring looks guilty. The dashboard now has automated tests that run before each release.
The Uno transmits at 5 V, so its line reaches the 3.3 V ESP32 through a divider.

name: SitSense
tag: A cushion that learns how one person sits before it judges their posture.
problem: Posture systems trained on pooled data lose accuracy on people they have never seen. Published results show drops from above 99% on known users to under 78% on new ones.
how: Eight force sensors, six in the seat and two in the backrest, are read through a multiplexer.
Two IMUs measure the tilt of the seat and the backrest.
A guided calibration records how each person sits, and thresholds are set relative to that person.
A rule-based detector flags sustained poor sitting, while a pressure-only detector runs alongside it on the same data as a comparison.
notes: Rules were chosen over machine learning because every threshold has to belong to one person.
A reversed sign in the left-right symmetry index made the detector silently never fire. It was found and fixed.
The whole study is planned as a 50-hour budget with hour-gated milestones instead of calendar dates.

name: Smart Temple
tag: A model temple that manages its own crowd, built for the World Robot Olympiad.
problem: Crowded temples need to know how many people are in each area and when to hold the gates. This model does it automatically.
how: Visitors carry RFID cards, and nine readers on one SPI bus track which zone each card is in.
Each zone has a visitor limit. Servo gates open and close to hold the count.
DC motors dispense prasadam and vibhuti.
The ESP32 splits Wi-Fi and control work across its two cores.
notes: I wrote two handbooks so Grade 4 and 5 students could follow the whole build: a 20-chapter general volume and a 25-page deep-dive that uses real values from the firmware.
Two characters, Robo and Guru Owl, carry the story through every chapter.

name: Ripening scan box
tag: Three ways of looking at a fruit, compared head to head.
problem: Artificially ripened fruit can look ripe outside while the inside lags behind. Which signal screens for it best: colour, near-infrared, or smell?
how: A portable box images bananas and tomatoes with a normal camera and with a NoIR camera under infrared light.
Two gas sensors sample the volatile compounds the fruit gives off.
Four models are compared: colour only, infrared only, gas only, and all three fused.
The output is a ripening mismatch score from 0 to 100 that sorts fruit into likely natural, suspicious or uncertain.
notes: It is framed as a screening tool. It makes no claim to detect specific chemicals.
A literature review of electronic-nose studies anchors the sensor choices.

name: Electronic nose for bananas
tag: Smelling the difference between natural and artificial ripening.
problem: Bananas ripened with chemical agents are sold as naturally ripened. The gases a banana gives off carry part of the story.
how: An MQ-3 follows ethanol, a by-product of ripening, and an MQ-135 follows ammonia and other volatiles.
Both are read through a 16-bit ADC into an ESP32.
Raw readings are converted to a resistance ratio and then to concentration using curve constants checked against the datasheets.
Bench runs on raw and ripe bananas provide the comparison data.
notes: Two firmware bugs were found and fixed: the clean-air calibration was off by a factor of 60 for one sensor, and the concentration equation was inverted.
The sensors output up to 5 V, so each analog line needs a divider before a 3.3 V input.
Humidity shifts these sensors more than anything else, which matters in Mumbai.
The build became a two-hour student session with a worksheet built from real bench data.

name: OvenEye
tag: A clip-on camera that tells you when the bake is done.
problem: Opening the oven door to check a bake drops the temperature, and timers do not know what the food looks like.
how: A camera pod hangs from the oven door handle and looks through the window.
A browning index is computed from pixel brightness, normalised against a white ceramic tile placed inside the oven.
A straight-line fit over the last six frames predicts the time left to the target colour.
The board serves its own Wi-Fi dashboard with snapshots and live readings.
notes: No machine learning is involved. The index is arithmetic and the estimate is a least-squares fit.
The mount is a three-part PETG pendant: a clamp on the handle, an arm, and the camera pod. Nothing rests on the glass.
A soft lip on the shroud blocks room reflections, with a vent notch so heat cannot build up.
The parts list comes to about ₹2,900.

name: Smart pet feeder
tag: Two bowls that know what was served and what was eaten.
problem: An automatic feeder can tell you it dispensed food. It cannot tell you whether the pet ate it.
how: Each bowl, one for dry food and one for water, sits on a load cell.
The feeder logs what went in and what is left, and the difference is what was consumed.
A small band on the pet reports movement and activity.
Everything shows up on a web dashboard.
notes: The band uses a XIAO ESP32C3 because it has battery charging built in.
Spillage and evaporation turned out to be good experiment-design problems for a young student.

name: Four-IMU body tracker
tag: Four motion sensors on a dancer, checked against a webcam.
problem: Is a camera good enough to analyse a pirouette, or do you need sensors on the body?
how: Four IMUs sit on the left and right shin, the spine and the head.
All four share one SPI bus on an ESP32 and stream orientation as quaternions over Wi-Fi.
The same movement is captured by a webcam and run through a pose-estimation model.
The two pipelines are compared.
notes: Getting four sensors to start reliably on one bus is the hard part and is still being worked on.

name: Water quality monitor
tag: A battery-powered probe set for turbidity, pH, dissolved solids and temperature.
problem: Cheap water sensors are easy to buy and easy to wire wrongly. Most output more voltage than an ESP32 pin can survive.
how: Turbidity and pH sensors feed the ESP32 through resistor dividers.
A dissolved-solids sensor and a waterproof temperature probe work together, so the reading is corrected for temperature.
A single lithium cell is boosted to 5 V for the sensors.
One status LED shows the state at a glance.
notes: All analog sensors sit on ADC1, because ADC2 stops working when Wi-Fi is on.
The firmware multiplies each divided reading by 1.5 to recover the true sensor voltage.

name: Folding-mast sensor head
tag: A robot mast that folds, with its sensors at the tip.
problem: When a mast folds, wires through the hinge fatigue and break. Spring contacts that only close when the mast is up avoid that, but ten contacts are hard to align.
how: A time-of-flight sensor and a lidar sit at the tip of the mast.
A small ESP32-C3 at the tip reads them and sends checksummed serial packets down.
That cuts the joint from ten contacts to four: power, ground and two data lines.
Pogo pins close the circuit only when the mast is fully deployed.
notes: A hinge drags pins sideways as it closes, which is the failure mode to design around.
Contact debouncing and switching the load on after the pins seat prevent arcing.

name: Flight controller panel
tag: A physical cockpit panel for a flight simulator.
problem: Flying a simulator from a keyboard hides the best part: flipping real switches.
how: Thirty-four toggle switches are read through I2C port expanders.
Rotary encoders and potentiometers cover the continuous controls.
An Arduino Leonardo presents the whole panel to the computer as a USB input device.
An OLED shows panel state.
notes: Built for the simulator Extreme Landings.
The Leonardo was chosen because it can act as a native USB device.

name: ESP32 arcade
tag: Ten games on one small screen.
problem: A good first big firmware project needs graphics, input, state and a menu. An arcade has all four.
how: An ESP32 drives a 2.4-inch colour display over SPI.
A menu launches about ten games, including Dino Run, Space Invaders, Frogger and Target Shoot.
Each game is its own state machine sharing the same input and drawing code.
notes: A strip of noise at the bottom of the screen came from the display library treating a 240×320 panel as 240×240. Fixing the driver configuration cleared it.

name: JamoBot
tag: Learn Korean letters by placing tiles on a robot.
problem: Hangul is built from letter blocks called jamo, which makes it a natural fit for physical tiles.
how: Learners place RFID letter tiles on the readers.
The ESP32 identifies the tile and responds with servo movement.
An OLED shows the Hangul.
notes: Built for the World Robot Olympiad.
Korean fonts overflowed the flash partition, and bitmap scaling had its own bugs. Most of the debugging went there.

name: Mecanum RC car
tag: Eight directions from one joystick.
problem: Mecanum wheels let a car slide sideways and diagonally, if you get the wheel mixing right.
how: An Arduino Nano reads the joystick and transmits over 433 MHz.
An Arduino Uno on the car decodes the direction and drives four motors.
A watchdog on the receiver guards the radio link.
notes: The eight directions come from a small lookup of wheel directions.

name: Voice colour picker
tag: Say a colour and the lights change. Built three different ways.
problem: There is more than one way to get speech into a microcontroller, and each has a catch.
how: First with an MIT App Inventor phone app.
Then with Python, offline speech recognition and a small web server.
Then with an ESP32 access point that uses the browser's own speech API.
notes: Full code exists for all three approaches, which makes it a useful comparison for students.

name: Wireless flight-sim controller
tag: A handheld controller and USB dongle from two ESP32-S3 boards.
problem: Commercial handheld flight controllers cost around $150. The same idea can be built from common parts.
how: One ESP32-S3 in the handheld reads sticks, sliders and switches.
It sends small packets over ESP-NOW to a second ESP32-S3 plugged into the computer.
The dongle appears as a standard USB joystick, so no drivers are needed.
notes: This one is still on paper. The mechanical parts, the rudder linkage and slider detents, are the hard part.

name: Heat shields for firefighting drones
tag: How to keep a multirotor alive near a fire.
problem: A drone that flies close to a fire is limited by how fast heat reaches its frame, motors and battery.
how: The paper draws on 28 published sources on plastics, aerogels, coatings and heat buffers.
It proposes a mass-specific figure of merit, Φ = 1/(kρ), that ranks insulation regardless of thickness.
A worked sizing case shows how to use it.
notes: A sign error in the absorbed-flux equation was found and corrected during revision.
A twelve-page manuscript was compressed to five pages with a 241-word abstract.

name: GeoPulse
tag: A live estimate of India's oil price next to a measure of world tension.
problem: Official figures for India's crude oil basket arrive late. A nowcast estimates the present from data that is already available.
how: A web app nowcasts the price of India's crude oil basket.
A geopolitical instability index is built from news.
The two are shown together and written up as a research paper.

name: µte
tag: Finding the sounds that trigger misophonia, and removing only those.
problem: For people with misophonia, ordinary sounds such as chewing can be unbearable. Blocking all sound is not a way to live.
how: Trigger sounds are detected in the audio stream.
Only those sounds are suppressed, and the rest of the soundscape is left alone.

name: DDoS mitigation in SDN
tag: Attacking a software-defined network to learn how to defend it.
problem: In a software-defined network one controller steers all traffic, so a flood aimed at it can take the whole network down.
how: I designed and analysed several DDoS attack scenarios.
I built and implemented a mitigation approach for SDN environments.
Packet drop during attacks fell by 94%.

name: NetCAD tool
tag: A network you can build, break and measure on a laptop.
problem: Testing a network design on real hardware is slow and expensive.
how: A custom topology of 8+ switches and 20+ hosts runs in Mininet.
Tests measure bandwidth, latency and packet loss.
Traffic is analysed live with sFlow-RT and Wireshark.

name: Backtesting framework
tag: Testing a trading strategy against prop-firm rules before risking the fee.
problem: A prop-firm challenge is a rule set as much as a market: daily loss limits, maximum drawdown, profit target. A strategy has to survive all of them at once.
how: Seven modules cover data, strategy, risk, rule enforcement, the engine and reporting.
The strategy is an EMA crossover with ATR-based stops across forex, indices and gold.
A challenge simulator enforces a 5% daily loss limit, 10% maximum drawdown, a 10% target and four minimum trading days.
Walk-forward validation tunes on the older half of the data, locks the parameters, and tests on the newer half.
notes: Walk-forward testing caught a textbook overfit: the optimiser's best setting had been chosen on only two trades.
Risk is fixed at 0.5% of the account per trade.

name: Cloud storefront on AWS
tag: A demo shop and the cloud design to host it.
problem: A working cart is the smallest thing that needs a server, a database and file storage together.
how: A demo shop with add-to-cart was written in HTML, CSS and JavaScript.
The proposed hosting put the site on EC2, the cart in DynamoDB behind Lambda functions, and static files in S3.

name: Bakery order system
tag: Orders in, confirmations out within five seconds.
problem: A small bakery taking orders by hand loses time and makes entry mistakes.
how: An order-entry screen takes customer details, order ID and billing.
Every order is logged to a spreadsheet.
The customer and the owner get an email and an SMS confirmation.
notes: Handles up to 100 orders a day.
